claim: Molecular bistables are strong candidates for long-term information storage, for example, in synaptic plasticity.
source: Molecular bistables are strong candidates for long-term information storage, for example, in synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is a general statement about molecular bistables supported by established scientific knowledge in the field of synaptic plasticity.

claim: Calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein Kinase II (CaMKII) is a highly expressed synaptic protein which has been proposed to form a molecular bistable switch capable of maintaining its state for years despite protein turnover and stochastic noise.
source: Calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein Kinase II (CaMKII) is a highly expressed synaptic protein which has been proposed to form a molecular bistable switch capable of maintaining its state for years despite protein turnover and stochastic noise.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior theoretical and modeling work in the field, as indicated by the broader context of the manuscript.

claim: CaMKII holoenzymes exchange subunits among themselves.
source: It has recently been shown that CaMKII holoenzymes exchange subunits among themselves.
evidence: This is stated as a recent experimental finding, implicitly referencing prior literature.

claim: Subunit exchange enhances information retention by CaMKII both by improving the stability of its switching in the PSD, and by slowing the decay of its activity in the spine cytosol.
source: Further, subunit exchange enhances information retention by CaMKII both by improving the stability of its switching in the PSD, and by slowing the decay of its activity in the spine cytosol.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by computational simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: CaMKII exhibits multiple timescales of activity due to subunit exchange.
source: We show that CaMKII exhibits multiple timescales of activity due to subunit exchange.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by computational modeling results.

claim: The existence of diverse timescales in the synapse has important theoretical implications for memory storage in networks.
source: The existence of diverse timescales in the synapse has important theoretical implications for memory storage in networks.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation based on the findings of the study and existing theoretical frameworks.

claim: Memories are believed to be stored in synapses, encoded as changes in synaptic strength.
source: Memories are believed to be stored in synapses, encoded as changes in synaptic strength (Hebb, 2005; Takeuchi et al., 2014; Choi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature in neuroscience.

claim: Long-term potentiation (LTP), an activity-dependent change in synaptic strength, is considered to be the primary post-synaptic memory mechanism.
source: Long-term potentiation (LTP), an activity-dependent change in synaptic strength, is considered to be the primary post-synaptic memory mechanism (Bliss and Collingridge, 2013; Mayford et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Various behavioral experiments strongly suggest a critical role for CaMKII in induction of LTP.
source: Various behavioral experiments strongly suggest a critical role for CaMKII in induction of LTP (Lucchesi et al., 2011; Giese et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: In the CA1 region of the hippocampus, blocking CaMKII activity blocks the induction of LTP.
source: In the CA1 region of the hippocampus, blocking CaMKII activity blocks the induction of LTP (Chang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: Recent evidence from behavioral assays suggests that CaMKII may also be involved in long-term maintenance of memory.
source: Recent evidence from behavioral assays suggests that CaMKII may also be involved in long-term maintenance of memory (Rossetti et al., 2017; but see Chang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent experimental studies, with a note of conflicting evidence.

claim: In the small volume of the synapse (∼0.02 µm3), the number of molecules involved in biochemical processes range from single digits to a few hundred, thereby increasing the effect of chemical noise.
source: In the small volume of the synapse (∼0.02 µm3 [Bartol et al., 2015]), the number of molecules involved in biochemical processes range from single digits to a few hundred, thereby increasing the effect of chemical noise.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on synaptic volume and by inference about molecular numbers.

claim: John Lisman proposed that a kinase and its phosphatase could form a bistable molecular switch able to maintain its state for a very long time despite turnover.
source: John Lisman proposed that a kinase and its phosphatase could form a bistable molecular switch able to maintain its state for a very long time despite turnover (Lisman, 1985).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lisman's theoretical work.

claim: It has been shown by various mathematical models that CaMKII and its phosphatase protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) may form a bistable switch which can retain its state for years despite stochastic chemical noise and protein turnover.
source: It has been shown by various mathematical models that CaMKII and its phosphatase protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) may form a bistable switch (Zhabotinsky, 2000) which can retain its state for years despite stochastic chemical noise and protein turnover (Miller et al., 2005; Hayer and Bhalla, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mathematical modeling studies.

claim: There is experimental evidence that CaMKII/PP1 is bistable in in vitro settings.
source: Although there is experimental evidence that CaMKII/PP1 is bistable in in vitro settings (Bradshaw et al., 2003; Urakubo et al., 2014), experimental evidence for in vivo bistability is lacking.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Experimental evidence for in vivo bistability of CaMKII/PP1 is lacking.
source: Although there is experimental evidence that CaMKII/PP1 is bistable in in vitro settings (Bradshaw et al., 2003; Urakubo et al., 2014), experimental evidence for in vivo bistability is lacking.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the experimental literature.

claim: In spine cytosol, CaMKII has been shown not to act like a bistable switch but rather a leaky integrator of calcium activity.
source: In spine cytosol, CaMKII has been shown not to act like a bistable switch but rather a leaky integrator of calcium activity (Chang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: CaMKII may be bistable in special micro-environments such as the 'core' PSD where it attaches to the NMDA receptor.
source: However, CaMKII may be bistable in special micro-environments such as the 'core' PSD where it attaches to the NMDA receptor (Dosemeci et al., 2016; Petersen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on PSD microenvironments.

claim: Previous modeling work has shown that the CaMKII/PP1 system may form a very stable switch despite protein turnover and stochastic noise in the small volume of the synapse.
source: Previous modeling work has shown that the CaMKII/PP1 system may form a very stable switch despite protein turnover and stochastic noise in the small volume of the synapse.
evidence: This is supported by references to prior modeling studies.

claim: The stability of the CaMKII/PP1 switch increases exponentially with the number of holoenzymes.
source: The stability increases exponentially with the number of holoenzymes (Miller et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a modeling study.

claim: The CaMKII/PP1 model exhibits bistable behavior only in a narrow range of PP1 concentrations in the PSD.
source: It is important to note that this model exhibits bistable behavior only in a narrow range of PP1 concentrations in the PSD.
evidence: This is a property of the model described in prior literature.

claim: Phosphorylated CaMKII is protected from phosphatases in PSD except PP1.
source: This strict restriction may be met because phosphorylated CaMKII is protected from phosphatases in PSD except PP1 (Strack et al., 1997a), which is tightly regulated in the PSD (Bollen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: PP1 is tightly regulated in the PSD.
source: This strict restriction may be met because phosphorylated CaMKII is protected from phosphatases in PSD except PP1 (Strack et al., 1997a), which is tightly regulated in the PSD (Bollen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study on PP1 regulation.

claim: Subunit exchange was hypothesized by Lisman but discovered only recently.
source: CaMKII has another remarkable property which was hypothesized by Lisman (Lisman, 1994) but discovered only recently, namely, subunit exchange.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lisman's hypothesis and recent experimental discovery.

claim: In the subunit exchange process, two CaMKII holoenzymes can exchange active subunits leading to spread of CaMKII activation.
source: In this process, two CaMKII holoenzymes can exchange active subunits leading to spread of CaMKII activation (Stratton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: The model without diffusion and without subunit exchange exhibited bistable behavior for CaMKII.
source: Without diffusion and subunit exchange, CaMKII in our model is bistable.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Switch stability (measured as average residence time in the stable states) increases exponentially with system size NCaMKII.
source: Switch stability (measured as average residence time in the stable states) increases exponentially with system size NCaMKII.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The fraction of time spent in intermediate states is much smaller when subunit exchange is enabled.
source: The fraction of time spent in intermediate states (dashed lines) is much smaller when subunit exchange is enabled (blue dashed line), that is the switching time is shorter.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Due to subunit exchange, relaxation time becomes independent of NPP1.
source: Due to subunit exchange, relaxation time becomes independent of NPP1 (blue vs red).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Without subunit exchange, switch stability decreases steeply with turnover rate.
source: Without subunit exchange, switch stability decreases steeply with turnover rate (red); however, when subunit exchange is enabled, switch stability is not affected by turnover rates as high as 1 h-1 (blue).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: When subunit exchange is enabled, switch stability is not affected by turnover rates as high as 1 h-1.
source: Without subunit exchange, switch stability decreases steeply with turnover rate (red); however, when subunit exchange is enabled, switch stability is not affected by turnover rates as high as 1 h-1 (blue).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the bistable regime, the number of switching events increases monotonically with turnover rate.
source: In the bistable regime (solid lines), the number of switching events increases monotonically with turnover rate.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Subunit exchange facilitated the spread of CaMKII activation.
source: As suggested in Stratton et al., 2014, we found that subunit exchange facilitated the spread of CaMKII activation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 4 and supported by citation.

claim: The effect of subunit exchange is greater (i.e. shorter rise times) at higher calcium levels for all values of Dsub.
source: The effect of subunit exchange is greater (i.e. shorter rise times) at higher calcium levels for all values of Dsub.
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Rise time is shorter for larger Dsub for all values of [Ca2+].
source: Rise time is also shorter for larger Dsub for all values of [Ca2+].
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The time to onset of CaMKII activity is independent of Dsub and depends only on [Ca2+].
source: The time to onset of CaMKII activity is independent of Dsub and depends only on [Ca2+].
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Subunit exchange does not play a significant role at the beginning of activation of CaMKII by Ca2+.
source: Average time for the onset of activity decreased with increasing basal [Ca2+] levels but remained independent of Dsub suggesting that subunit exchange does not play a significant role at the beginning of activation of CaMKII by Ca2+.
evidence: This is an inference from simulation results shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The population of clustered CaMKII acted as a single bistable switch when subunit exchange was enabled.
source: The population of clustered CaMKII acted as a single bistable switch (Figure 5B, blue plot).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The synchronization effect was strong and robust to variation in Dsub.
source: This effect was strong and robust to variation in Dsub.
evidence: This is an interpretation of simulation results.

claim: Even for a very small value of Dsub = 0.01 µm2 s−1, strong synchronization was observed.
source: Even for a very small value of Dsub = 0.01 µm2 s−1, we observed strong synchronization (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Subunit exchange may account for the observed dual decay rate of CaMKII phosphorylation.
source: Finally, we asked if subunit exchange might account for the complex time-course of CaMKII dynamics in spine as observed in recent experiments (Chang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by simulations and comparison with experimental data.

claim: Enabling diffusion of CaMKII subunits and PP1 decreased the rate of dephosphorylation roughly by a factor of 5.
source: We then enabled the diffusion of CaMKII subunits (Dsub = 1 µm2 s−1) and PP1 (DPP1 = 0.5 µm2 s−1). These conditions decreased the rate of dephosphorylation roughly by a factor of 5 (41.65 s vs. 200.82 s) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by simulation results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A mixed population of clustered and non-clustered CaMKII should decay with two time-constants.
source: Therefore a mixed population of clustered and non-clustered CaMKII should decay with two time-constants.
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claim: The time-constants obtained from simulations (8.4 s, 86.2 s) matched well with experimentally estimated time-constants of (6.4 s ± 0.7, 92.6 s ± 50.7).
source: The time-constants obtained (8.4 s, 86.2 s) matched well with experimentally estimated time-constants of (6.4 s ± 0.7, 92.6 s ± 50.7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison of simulation results with experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Subunit exchange strongly affects the properties of the CaMKII/PP1 pathway, both in its role as a bistable switch in the PSD and as a leaky integrator of Ca2+ activity in spine cytosol.
source: Here, we have shown that subunit exchange strongly affects the properties of the CaMKII/PP1 pathway, both in its role as a bistable switch in the PSD and as a leaky integrator of Ca2+ activity in spine cytosol.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: In the PSD, subunit exchange improved the stability of the CaMKII/PP1 switch by synchronizing the kinase activity across the PSD.
source: In the PSD, where the model was tuned to elicit bistable dynamics from clustered CaMKII, subunit exchange improved the stability of the CaMKII/PP1 switch by synchronizing the kinase activity across the PSD (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on simulation results shown in Figure 6 (likely referring to Figure 5).

claim: Subunit exchange improved active CaMKII tolerance of PP1, and of turnover rate.
source: It also improved active CaMKII tolerance of PP1, and of turnover rate (Figure 2 and Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on simulation results shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: In the case where CaMKII was uniformly distributed in PSD, subunit exchange facilitated more rapid activation of CaMKII.
source: In the case where CaMKII was uniformly distributed in PSD, subunit exchange facilitated more rapid activation of CaMKII (Figure 4B–D) (Stratton et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on simulation results shown in Figure 4 and supported by citation.

claim: A CaMKII mutant lacking subunit exchange would be deficient in switch stability and slower to be activated by Ca2+.
source: These simulation results predict that a CaMKII mutant lacking subunit exchange would be deficient in switch stability and slower to be activated by Ca2+, thereby resulting in degraded memory retention and deficient learning in memory-related behavioral experiments, respectively.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the simulation results.

claim: In the spine head, subunit exchange facilitated integration by prolonging the decay time-course of kinase activity.
source: In the spine head, subunit exchange facilitated integration by prolonging the decay time-course of kinase activity (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on simulation results shown in Figure 6.

claim: CaMKII dynamics changed from an integrator to bistable switch as we moved from spine cytosol to the PSD.
source: The fact that CaMKII dynamics changed from an integrator to bistable switch as we moved from spine cytosol (a phosphatase rich environment) to the PSD (where PP1 is tightly controlled) suggests an interesting sub-compartmentalization of functions in these microdomains.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results.

claim: Clustering of CaMKII had important implications for its sustained activity.
source: Furthermore, we observed that the clustering of CaMKII had important implications for its sustained activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on simulation results.

claim: Subunit exchange is unlikely to have any impact on neighbouring spines.
source: Subunit exchange is unlikely to have any impact on neighbouring spines.
evidence: This is based on calculations of escape time and dephosphorylation rates.

claim: The mean escape time of a single CaMKII subunit from a typical spine is between 8 s to 33 s.
source: The mean escape time of a single CaMKII subunit from a typical spine is between 8 s to 33 s (Holcman and Schuss, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a theoretical study.

claim: Any phosphorylated subunit is almost certain to be de-phosphorylated by PP1 during the escape time from the spine.
source: Any phosphorylated subunit is almost certain to be de-phosphorylated by PP1 during this time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the escape time and known dephosphorylation rates.

claim: The effects of synchronization are local to each PSD, where PP1 is known to be tightly controlled.
source: We therefore predict that the effects of synchronization are local to each PSD, where PP1 is known to be tightly controlled.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the simulation results and known properties of the PSD.

claim: Subunit exchange loses its potency in the phosphatase rich region of the bulk spine head or dendrite.
source: Subunit exchange loses its potency in the phosphatase rich region of the bulk spine head or dendrite.
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation results and known properties of different cellular compartments.

claim: CaMKII subunit exchange is unlikely to play any role in intra-spine information exchange such as synaptic tagging.
source: We therefore consider it unlikely that CaMKII subunit exchange plays any role in intra-spine information exchange such as synaptic tagging.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of escape times and dephosphorylation.

claim: CaMKII is non-uniformly distributed in the PSD where it is mostly concentrated in a small region of 16 nm to 36 nm below the synaptic cleft.
source: CaMKII is non-uniformly distributed in the PSD where it is mostly concentrated in a small region of 16 nm to 36 nm below the synaptic cleft (Petersen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: In the PSD, CaMKII may exist in large clusters given that the PSD is rich in CaMKII binding partners.
source: In the PSD, CaMKII may exist in large clusters given that the PSD is rich in CaMKII binding partners.
evidence: This is an inference based on known properties of the PSD.

claim: Subunit exchange may lead to synchronization when CaMKII is clustered, or more rapid activation by Ca2+ when it is uniformly distributed.
source: Our study predicts that subunit exchange may lead to synchronization when CaMKII is clustered, or more rapid activation by Ca2+ when it is uniformly distributed.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the simulation results.

claim: The existence of diverse time-scales of CaMKII activity has important theoretical implications.
source: Finally, we suggest that the existence of diverse time-scales of CaMKII activity – bistable and highly stable synchronized bistable in PSD, slow and fast decaying leaky integrator in spine head (Table 1) – has important theoretical implications.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the findings.

claim: A theoretical meta-model which sought to strike a balance between learning and memory retention requires that a diversity of timescales must exist at the synapse for optimum performance.
source: A theoretical meta-model which sought to strike a balance between these two competing demands requires that a diversity of timescales must exist at the synapse (Benna and Fusi, 2016) for optimum performance.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a theoretical study.

claim: The Benna and Fusi model requires the memory trace to be first stored in a fast variable and then progressively and efficiently transferred to slower variables.
source: This model requires the memory trace to be first stored in a fast variable and then progressively and efficiently transferred to slower variables.
evidence: This is a description of the requirements of the theoretical model.

claim: The study suggests a concrete mechanism for progressive transfer of memory traces from fast to slow variables.
source: Our study suggests a concrete mechanism for such a process.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation connecting the study's findings to existing theory.

claim: The Ca2+ concentration in the PSD can be mapped to the fastest variable in the memory storage model.
source: Here, the Ca2+ concentration in the PSD can be mapped to the fastest variable.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the findings.

claim: The CaMKII integrator in the cytosol could represent the second slower variable to which the trace is transferred from Ca2+.
source: The CaMKII integrator in the cytosol could represent the second slower variable to which the trace is transferred from Ca2+.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the findings.

claim: The state information is transferred to the third slower CaMKII bistable switch.
source: Further, the state information is transferred to the third slower CaMKII bistable switch.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the findings.

claim: The dynamics of CaMKII in the PSD forms an even slower bistable variable for longer retention of the memory trace.
source: The dynamics of CaMKII in the PSD forms an even slower bistable variable for longer retention of the memory trace.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the findings.

claim: The model treats the CaMKII ring as a proxy for the CaMKII holoenzyme.
source: We treat the CaMKII ring as a proxy for the CaMKII holoenzyme, which consists of two such rings stacked over each other (Woodgett et al., 1983; Hoelz et al., 2003; Chao et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a modeling assumption supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Active CaMKII is defined as a holoenzyme (ring of six or seven subunits) in which at least two subunits are phosphorylated at Thr286.
source: We define Active CaMKII as a holoenzyme (ring of six or seven subunits) in which at least two subunits are phosphorylated at Thr286.
evidence: This is a definition used in the model.

claim: In the model, CaMKII exists in 15 possible states compared to two in the MZ model.
source: In our model, CaMKII exists in 15 possible states compared to two in the MZ model (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the model structure.

claim: The model replaced the Michaelis-Menten approximation in the MZ model by equivalent mass-action kinetics.
source: We also replaced the Michaelis-Menten approximation in the MZ model by equivalent mass-action kinetics (e.g. Equation 2).
evidence: This is a description of a modeling choice.

claim: The resting Ca2+ level in spine is 80 nM.
source: We assumed the resting Ca2+ level in spine to be 80 nM (Berridge, 1998).
evidence: This is a modeling assumption supported by a citation.

claim: All simulations were performed using the stochastic solver based on the Gillespie method, in the MOOSE simulator.
source: All simulations were performed using the stochastic solver based on the Gillespie method, in the MOOSE simulator (https://moose.ncbs.res.in, version 3.1.4; Ray and Bhalla, 2008).
evidence: This is a description of the computational methods used.

claim: The discretized system converges to reference bistable for DPP1 ≥ 0.5µm2s-1.
source: The discretized system converges to reference bistable for DPP1 ≥ 0.5µm2s-1 (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by validation results shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The long-term behavior of discretized system was most sensitive to DPP1 and almost independent of Dsub.
source: The long-term behavior of discretized system was most sensitive to DPP1 (Figure 8B) and almost independent of Dsub (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by validation results shown in Figures 8A and 8B.
